title: Breaking and Entering: Jazmine Mary on Art, Inner Critics and Radical Acts
transcript:
A conversation with Jazmine Mary, broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 11 June 2026.

On RRR you're with Lauren. We heard at the top from an album that came out last week from the Bristol trio Tara Clerkin Trio.

Somewhere Good is the name of the new record and we heard the track Silently.

And just then from an artist who, well it's with me in the RRR studios as we speak,

Jazmine Mary who is in town playing tonight at the Merri Creek Tavern.

I believe there's a low ticket warning on that if you want to head along.

We heard back of the bar from Jazmine's release of last year on the iconic Flying Nun label.

I Want to Rock and Roll is the name of the record.

And a pleasure to have you joining me on Breaking and Entering Jazmine.

Thanks for having me.

It's lovely to have you here and as well as playing tonight you played over the weekend.

We were just chatting about Rising's Day Tripper festival that you were a part of which is kind of like a festival within a festival.

Did you manage to stick around at Day Tripper and catch any of the other acts?

Yeah, I watched Kae Tempest.

I'm a big fan.

That was awesome.

And Xiao Xiao was one of the other ones I watched the entire set of which was really, really fun.

I hadn't seen them before.

Yeah, cool.

Yeah.

And being in Melbourne for I guess the last few days now.

Well you're originally, you're based in New Zealand now but I was surprised to learn that you're originally from Australia.

You grew up in…

Yeah, I grew up in Gippsland.

In Gippsland.

Yeah.

And you lived in Melbourne for a little while.

A couple of years when I was like 18, 19.

Had a bit too much fun.

Yeah.

Being back here, I guess, are there things that you like to do or places that are special to you like to visit where that you've returned to on this trip?

I was actually looking at like [name uncertain: DeGrave Street] or something where I met like my first girlfriend when I was like 18 and then the grilled next door where she dumped me like six months later.

It's okay.

I'll be all right.

It was a long time ago.

But it was funny walking around and seeing these little places of like baby me.

Yeah.

Yeah.

I did see on stories, you played in Ballarat yesterday as well.

I saw that you stopped in at the iconic pancake parlor, pancake kitchen.

Yeah.

Well, you should have stopped out the front.

Oh, you did.

You didn't go in.

I was going to ask you about, yeah, your pancake order.

But when, I guess, yeah, when did you make that move across the ditch to New Zealand?

How long ago was that?

Maybe like I would have been 21, so yeah, 2012 or something or 14.

Yeah.

Yeah, it's quite a while ago.

Yeah.

You've spoken about, I guess, how you've, you never really discovered a music community until you moved to Aotearoa.

Can you tell me about, I guess, that musical community you connected with and what was it about the local scene and the environment there that finally made you feel connected?

I mean, I think Gippsland, Trafalgar specifically, the town I'm from, is so small.

Like there's not, there's no bands, there's no music.

And if there is, it was like dudes in like screamo bands maybe in like two towns over.

So the idea of being a musician didn't even really exist other than like going on Australian Idol or something like that.

You know, real small town brain.

And then moved to Melbourne and was just culture shocked.

Like little town kid, I was like, whoa, I felt so out of my depth.

And like I said, just got up to a bunch of nonsense for a few years.

And so I think when I moved to New Zealand, I started to find community and people and like I played guitar and stuff, but I think I found people there that were really encouraging.

Like there's some experimental nights I'd go to and sort of join in and people just kept saying to play or inviting me to or collaborating.

And, you know, it just slowly happened and all of a sudden I was doing it all the time.

Yeah.

So it was quite a lovely way to grow into a musician, I think.

And you mentioned, yeah, when you're creating music that you're like extremely impulsive and intuitive.

Like you create music quite quickly to stay ahead of your critical self that you said.

I guess, yeah, many creators or just many people get sort of completely paralyzed by their inner critic.

Do you have any advice, I guess, for artists who may want to learn how to move faster than their own self-doubt?

Yeah.

I don't know if you have to move quickly to get away from self-doubt.

But I think being around people that make you feel incredible.

Like my band are really supportive and all my friends, they will make me feel like I can do anything.

And that's really nice, you know, so they can lift me up really, really too high.

And then my inner critic will smash me back down enough to sort of central.

But having good people around you that are supportive and that celebrate your wins, I think, is massive.

Totally.

Given you like to sort of work in that really kind of impulsive way and enjoy improvisation as well,

are there any like happy accident moments that make their way onto this new album?

Oh, heaps of stuff.

Like even a lot of the production stuff is like kind of going into the studio with, you know, 50% of the songs done.

Like the bones of it and then leaving space for improvisation or things to change.

I think a lot of the like vocal things that happen, because I like to do one or two takes,

a lot of the woos or like sometimes I can hear maybe I can hear myself smiling and things or

yeah, or stuff like that or just like sort of little ritual or practice to get into a present state while recording.

Like that stuff that I can hear in the song that's quite nice, like a candle burning that I know is happening, you know.

Yeah, but lots of happy accidents.

In terms of where you like where you do a lot of your writing, you've said that you sing along, sing a lot in the car and have sort of do a lot of voice memos in the car as well.

Do you find, I don't know, the rhythm of driving or just being alone in the car helps the melodies or ideas like flow better?

I think it's like the only time I'm in quiet.

Like I do not, I don't like listening to music in the car really.

And I think, yeah, I think it's like I have a really busy life and I'm sure a lot of people relate to that as like when you're in the car, you're there, you're in your box and you're flying down a highway and you can't do anything else.

So I feel like that's kind of when my mind creatively frees up where I'm like processing my thoughts and feelings, all of those things.

So, and no one can hear you.

So like scream singing or like sounding stupid, I don't know, there's like a real protectiveness to the car so that no one can catch you.

It's too quick or something.

Safe space.

Yeah.

Do you have any like daily rituals that are important to you in terms of your creative practice?

Maybe not daily.

Like I just try and do it all the time.

I write a lot like when I'm in a connected space, like if I'm connected to myself, I try and write a lot, which happens less when touring because you're, you know, we're all in the car together and then sleeping together and then eating together.

And I love it, but there's less time for creativity then.

But yeah, going outside, being in nature, just all that, all that cliche stuff.

That's a cliche for a reason, you know, anything that helps me listen to myself is going to help me be able to create.

I wanted to bring up, I guess, there was a really insightful article you wrote for Rolling Stone recently, which is for their Making Music, Making Ends Meet, a new series that they're sort of focusing on musicians during the cost of living crisis.

And you said to remain an artist is a radical act.

Can I ask, what is it about making music and art right now that makes it feel radical for you?

I think even the, like a real conservative response to me saying like, to be an artist right now as a radical act is like, no, it's not.

Buckle up, what happened to rock and roll?

Like this is some of the boomer responses to this thing.

I think doing something hopeful and doing something meaningful and that music and art is usually a space where people are wanting change, you know, like we're all playing fundraiser shows for a free Palestine.

We're all, we're all activists.

We're all trying to help, um, free each other and that I don't really know many artists that aren't doing that.

Um, and to do that when getting paid fuck all and being told you're ungrateful at the same time by a certain group of people.

Yeah, it is a radical act and it's just radical to remain hopeful and loving, like to be hopeless right now is a very powerful fascist tool.

Like it's all, it's, it's, um, it's very indulgent to say, you know, well, it's not going to do anything.

So I won't do anything.

I think that's extremely lazy.

Um, and yeah, it's just brave to feel in this world, isn't it right now?

Like, you know, you've also said your art is like a way to understand yourself and also to be understood.

And I guess I'm curious, what did you learn about yourself through the making of your latest record?

Hmm.

I think if I knew how to articulate that so well in words, I wouldn't write the music.

So I don't know if I know how to, um, articulate that exactly.

And it's always changing and I can't always mark it.

I think I'm still in the process of learning what that is, but I think I'm just, uh, constantly getting kinder toward myself, which is,

you know, it's no small feat, um, and therefore kinder to the world around me.

Um, yeah, I don't know.

I just getting, getting closer to, I don't know, just having a fucking weird, nice time, you know?

Yeah.

Taking the right thing seriously and the other stuff not.

Yeah.

Yeah.

That's a beautiful thing.

You mentioned sharing your work and, um, talking to people, um, helps you get to understand what you're doing.

Like when you're making it, you don't really sort of understand what you're doing, kind of an interesting sort of internal creation versus that external discovery, I guess.

It's in a sense, like, does it feel like you're experiencing your own work for the first time only after you release it to everyone else?

I think it just changes.

So it's like, it's mine and I'm doing it and experiencing whatever that is.

And then as soon as you share it, it kind of becomes everyone else's, right?

And then there's no way to ever go back to the source of creating it because someone, someone the other day was like, I was so heartbroken and I was listening to all of those songs.

And for them, that was that, that thing.

That wasn't my, well, you know, uh, so I think as soon as it leaves the body, it just takes on a million forms.

And that's what's so cool about it, like about anyone's art or music, right?

Is that it can just, um, yeah, kind of get the ownership goes.

It's interesting, yeah, that, I guess, how that dialogue with an audience can, yeah, kind of reveal meaning in your work.

Do you think, um, does an artist like need an audience to truly understand like their own creation, do you think?

Nah, surely not, right?

I don't think so.

I'd hate, I'd hate to, I'd hate to say that.

No, I don't think so.

I was intrigued when you said, um, as well about your music that you like confusing people, but you also like feeling confused and figuring it out.

Yeah.

Um, yeah, do you, I don't know, do you intentionally sort of like engineer moments of confusion to challenge yourself in any sort of way?

Like, do you enjoy problem solving or being like a puzzle in a way?

No, God, no, it's all hard enough without putting effort into that.

But I think, um, just goes back to acting on that impulse and being like, it's art, you know, so it can be really, really sincere, but it can also be a lie and be sincere at the same time.

Like it's all, it's all made up and it's all real.

Um, and maybe the reason I talked about confusing people and being confused is because I get asked some very literal questions about things I do a lot and find it really hard to know how to answer those without being boring.

You know, like, you know, like, what does the album title mean?

And it's like, well, man, I don't know.

Lucky I didn't have that on my list of questions for you.

Yeah, no, well, I assumed not.

Um, I want to say, yeah, a very big thank you to my guest, Jazmine Mary, who's been joining me today.

And, uh, yeah, you can catch Jazmine tonight at the Merri Creek Tavern, which should be a really special show.

And you're off to Canberra tomorrow.

That's it.

If you've got any friends there, please send them along.

Um, and do check out, um, Jazmine Mary's, um, amazing videos as well.

They're really, um, quite gorgeous.

And we were chatting off air saying there's a connection with, um, the bats with those videos.

Oh, [name uncertain: Annabelle Keane], yeah, whose parents are in the bats.

And Annabelle does most of those, um, videos with me.

Does a great job.

Yeah.

That's very cool.

Uh, you've also mentioned, yeah, each song on the record sort of occupies its own emotional space.

I've lined up, um, yeah, the track Memphis, uh, to play.

What kind of, yeah, emotional space would you say that this track occupies?

Oh, that was, um, there's not normally a story, but that was a, like, [name uncertain: Lynn, Lynn Mall], like a West Auckland Mall.

And I was so fucking depressed.

And I was crying, crying, crying in the car.

And you know when you're, like, in that void of such sadness, you don't know what to do with your body.

So I went into the mall to get a mall massage.

I was, like, zombie, zombying through life, like I didn't know what to do.

And I went in to get this massage.

And walking in Memphis was, like, bleeding in through the mall with this, like, meditation music that was also on.

And it was super trippy because of my state.

And I was laying on my back, and I opened my eyes, and the masseuse looked at me and said,

It's okay.

I can see you now.

You can relax.

And that just made me feel, I don't know.

It was a very spiritual experience at the mall.

I love that.

Yeah.

This is Memphis from Jazmine Mary.

Thanks so much, Jazmine.

Thanks for having me.

Pleasure.
